                                                        Abstract
          Recent work in random matrix theory (RMT) has developed the notion of deterministic equiva-
     lents: typically linear surrogate models that approximate the spectral behavior of large nonlinear
     random matrices, such as nonlinear feature maps in neural networks (NNs). Such equivalents make
     theoretical predictions tractable by reducing a complex model to a simpler one with properties
     that fall under the umbrella of classical RMT tools. However, this leaves open the question of
     whether this idealized linear equivalence remains meaningful for classification of high-dimensional
     nonlinearly separable data. Motivated by this, we consider the conjugate kernel (CK), which is
     the nonlinear feature map of a one-layer feedforward NN, under a canonical nonlinearly separable
     dataset for the XOR problem; and we use the study of informative outlier eigenvalues in the CK
     and whether their corresponding eigenvectors asymptotically align with XOR labels as a proxy for
     nonlinear learnability. We develop a robust quadratic equivalent of the CK matrix that enables a
     precise analysis of emergent informative spikes, as one modifies various knobs common in ML
     practice: sample complexity, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), nonlinear activation choice, and pretrained
     features. We identify regimes in which these knobs move the CK beyond the linear equivalent
     and produce BBP-type transitions to label-aligned outlier eigenspaces. Our analysis helps bring
     deterministic-equivalence tools from RMT to bear on problems of practical relevance in ML.
     Keywords: Conjugate kernel; random features; random matrix theory; BBP phase transition;
     deterministic equivalents; spectral clustering; Gaussian Equivalence Theory; XOR problem.


1. Introduction
Spectral information from weight matrices, kernel matrices, and Hessians provides a quantitative
window into representation learning and efficient optimization in neural networks (NNs) (Martin and
Mahoney, 2021, 2019, 2020; Martin et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Jacot et al.,
2018; Pennington and Worah, 2017; Adlam and Pennington, 2020; Liao and Mahoney, 2021; Sagun
et al., 2016; Ghorbani et al., 2019a). For example, eigenvalues of NN weight matrices can capture
the strength of learned directions, while the corresponding eigenvectors indicate which data features
are amplified or extracted during training (Ba et al., 2022; Damian et al., 2022; Moniri et al., 2023;
Dandi et al., 2024). A major direction in deep learning theory is to use spectral tools to understand
when NNs can propagate, preserve, transform, or amplify task-relevant structure that may be hidden
in high-dimensional datasets.

     A concrete and widely used spectral mechanism is the emergence of spikes (outlier eigen/singular
values) and the alignment of their eigen/singular vectors with signals in the dataset. Random matrix
theory (RMT) provides a powerful tool to analyze such eigen-spike emergence. In high-dimensional
spiked models where a low-rank signal is embedded in Gaussian noise, BBP (Baik–Ben Arous–
Péché) phase transitions characterize when an informative outlier separates from the bulk spectrum
and when its associated eigenvector becomes correlated with the underlying signal (Baik et al., 2005;
Nadler, 2008). Recent work has developed nonlinear counterparts for random-feature and kernel-type
matrices, providing sharp predictions for outlier locations and eigenvector alignment (Feldman, 2023;
Ba et al., 2022, 2023; Wang et al., 2024). Such nonlinear RMT can be applied to study deep learning
theory, e.g., the infinite-width Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) and the Conjugate Kernel (CK) (Jacot
et al., 2018; Pennington and Worah, 2017; Adlam and Pennington, 2020) for multi-layer NNs. Their
high-dimensional spectra have been studied extensively (Liao and Mahoney, 2025; Wang and Zhu,
2024; Liao et al., 2020). In this work, we focus on the CK, and we study emergent spikes induced by
nonlinear structure in the data. Concretely, we consider the following spectral question for CK:
      When can NNs transfer a nonlinear pattern in the data into a linearly accessible direction
      (an aligned eigen-spike) that enables linear classification?
    In this paper, the CK is defined by a one-hidden-layer random NN: Y = √1N σ(W X) ∈ RN ×n ,
with nonlinear activation σ, random weights W ∈ RN ×d , and data X ∈ Rd×n . The CK matrix is the
Gram matrix of hidden activations, K = Y ⊤ Y ∈ Rn×n for n data points. The spectral distribution
of K is particularly useful for generalization error of random feature regression, as demonstrated in
Mei and Montanari (2022); Hu and Lu (2022) for isotropic Gaussian data X. However, real datasets
often contain low-rank or nonlinear structure that may be hard to analyze using PCA (Jolliffe, 2002;
Schölkopf et al., 1998; Tenenbaum et al., 2000; Roweis and Saul, 2000; Belkin and Niyogi, 2003;
Coifman and Lafon, 2006; Johnstone and Lu, 2009). To highlight genuinely nonlinear structure, we
instead take X to be the high-dimensional XOR Gaussian mixture dataset (Section 3). This dataset is
a balanced four-component Gaussian mixture whose two classes are unions of opposite components
(Refinetti et al., 2021). The key property is that XOR is not linearly separable in first-order statistics:
the class means vanish, and any method that only “sees” linear correlations cannot recover labels.
However, XOR is quadratically separable, so a second-order feature can potentially make the task
linearly solvable. Heuristically, the eigenvalues of K describe the spectrum of learned similarities,
while the alignment of leading eigenvectors with task structure (e.g., labels or cluster indicators) may
lead to spectral methods solving the task. Therefore, this paper aims to answer the following spectral
question for K:
      When do outlier eigenvalues emerge in the CK spectrum, and when do their spiked
      eigenvectors align with the XOR labels and enable linear classification?
    In practice, NN performance is affected by hyperparameters, dataset structure, and architecture;
and, as a practical matter, machine learning (ML) practitioners typically fiddle (quite aggressively)
with various “knobs” of the ML training process in order to improve model performance. Motivated
by this, we consider properties of the CK matrix for the XOR problem, as various “knobs” for K are
varied; and, depending on their values, we observe very different spectral behavior. Concretely, we
vary the following knobs (which are among the standard parameters that are tuned in ML practice):
sampling size scaling n with input features d and NN width N ; signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the
data X; the pretrained weight matrix W ; and the choice of nonlinear activation σ. We show that,

1.1. Our Approach
Much of the existing RMT literature on the CK matrix analysis lies in a proportional regime
(n ≍ d ≍ N ), and it often involves the assumption of isotropic Gaussian data Z ∈ Rd×n . In
this setting, a standard tool is a linear equivalent (LE) for the nonlinear feature matrix σ(W Z).
This approach replaces the nonlinear features with an affine Gaussian surrogate and an independent
Gaussian noise term N :
                                                                   i.i.d.
                      σ(W Z) ≈ bσ W Z + aσ N ,                Nij ∼ N (0, 1),                     (1.1)

for constants aσ , bσ determined by σ. This approximation is also called Gaussian equivalence in
prior work (Mei and Montanari, 2022; Hu and Lu, 2022; Goldt et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2023).
When applying the LE, one can show that the spectra of nonlinear CK matrices are asymptotically
equivalent to a linear model, thus making classical RMT directly applicable. However, the LE also
suggests that the induced kernel behaves essentially like a linear kernel plus isotropic noise; this can
hide important nonlinear task structure. Figure 1 shows that CK matrix with LE resembles a linear

    For the XOR problem, the nonlinearity σ is essential: it can transform a nonlinear classification
task into one that is linearly accessible. To understand this, we vary the ML “knobs” listed above
to identify regimes in which the LE approximation works, versus when it breaks down. To go
beyond the classical LE in (1.1), we develop a refined (quadratic) equivalent model that captures
emergent spiked eigenvalues and eigenvectors carrying nonlinear information about CK and the
dataset, thereby enabling linear classification on the nonlinear XOR problem. We refer to such spikes
as quadratic informative spikes. Addressing these questions will clarify the regimes in which NNs,
and in particular various choices for training knobs of the ML training process, can recover and even
amplify beneficial nonlinear features concealed in the dataset.
Quadratic equivalents (QE). We model the XOR data as a low-rank perturbation X = Z + M ,
where Z is Gaussian noise and M is a rank-two signal that encodes the XOR structure. Our goal is
to understand how this signal shows up in the CK spectrum. We go beyond the LE in (1.1), which
captures only the bulk spectrum, and derive a QE that precisely tracks all spikes via a second-order
Taylor approximation of σ. At a high level, this yields the decomposition

                  σ(W X) ≈             σ(W Z)                +       T1          +        T2            (1.2)
                                       | {z }                       |{z}                 |{z}
                                 bulk+uninformative spikes       linear spikes       quadratic spikes

where T1 and T2 are finite-rank contributions induced by the signal M and σ (see (A.1) and
Proposition 10). In this QE, there are three terms. The first term, σ(W Z), determines the bulk
spectrum; and it may also possibly induce uninformative outliers, solely due to the architecture
(Benigni and Péché, 2022). The second term, T1 , corresponds to a linear transformation of the signal
M ; while it can induce outliers, their eigenvectors turn out not to be aligned with the XOR labels,
meaning that they are not useful for nonlinear XOR classification. The third term, T2 , captures
quadratic properties: depending on the correct tuning of the ML training “knobs,” this quadratic
term T2 can dominate and create quadratic informative spikes (see (A.1)). This effectively provides
a “quadratic feature channel” that makes the nonlinear XOR problem analyzable with RMT and
linearly separable. In Appendix A, we present the formal statement of this QE and the proof strategy
of our main results.

1.2. Our Contributions
We develop a RMT framework for the CK that is based on a QE and that captures when nonlinear
learnability emerges for XOR, in regimes where the LE behavior is insufficient. We are particularly
interested in this emergence as a function of the following four “knobs” that are widely-used by ML
practitioners (see Table 1).
1. Finite-SNR proportional limit (n ≍ d): negative results. In the proportional regime with
   SNR = Θ(1), CK can exhibit outlier eigenvalues, but their eigenvectors do not align with
   XOR labels; hence spectral methods with linear readouts on CK features fail to classify XOR
   (Theorem 3; Figure 1). We also prove failure for spectral clustering of Euclidean distance kernel.
2. Large-SNR proportional limit: emergence of quadratic informative spike. We prove that with
   increasing SNR scaling and with proper activation choice, a quadratic informative outlier separates
   and aligns with the XOR labels, enabling linear spectral clustering/classification (Theorem 7).

2. Additional Literature Review
Simplicity bias and low-rank structure. Recent work suggests that deep networks and transform-
ers exhibit an implicit distributional simplicity bias, learning simpler (lower-order) statistical structure
of the data earlier in training (Belrose et al., 2024; Rende et al., 2024). Complementarily, Huh et al.
(2023) report a low-rank simplicity bias in deep networks, arguing that depth/over-parameterization
can implicitly favor low effective-rank feature representations. From a broader perspective, Wilson
(2025) argues that many generalization phenomena often viewed as “mysterious” in deep learning
can be reconciled with classical theory via soft inductive biases.
Spectrum of kernel random matrices. The study of kernel random matrices and their spectral
distributions has become a major topic in RMT. Global convergence of the empirical spectral
distribution (ESD) is known for broad classes of nonlinear kernels (El Karoui, 2010; Cheng and
Singer, 2013; Do and Vu, 2013). In the proportional regime, Cheng and Singer (2013) and Do and
Vu (2013) characterize limiting spectra of inner-product kernels. The CK and NTK can be viewed as
random kernels, whose spectra were further studied (Fan and Wang, 2020; Adlam and Pennington,
2020; Péché, 2019; Pennington and Worah, 2017; Dabo and Male, 2024; Guionnet and Piccolo, 2026)
and connected to generalization in random feature regression (Mei and Montanari, 2022; Adlam and
Pennington, 2020) and memorization of spurious feature (Bombari and Mondelli, 2024) .
Nonlinear spiked covariance matrices. Spiked models exhibit phase transitions where informative
eigenvalues separate from the bulk (Baik et al., 2005; Péché, 2006). Recent work extends this to
nonlinear random matrices, i.e., matrices whose entries are nonlinear functions of high-dimensional
random projections (such as σ(W X)), leading to nonlinear analogues of BBP transitions and

alignment formulas (Wang and Zhu, 2024; Feldman, 2023; Ba et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024;
Guionnet et al., 2023; Benigni and Péché, 2022). Outlier eigenstructure of CK and NTK has been
studied Li et al. (2025), using the deterministic equivalence from Gu et al. (2022). Although they can
deal with random deep networks and general Gaussian mixture datasets, their CKs and NTKs are
expected kernels (namely first take width N → ∞) and only equivalent to linear kernels.
Polynomial sample-size regimes. In the proportional regime (n ≍ d), LE/Gaussian-equivalence
phenomena often imply linear-kernel behavior for broad families of kernels. Moving to polynomial
regimes (n ≍ dk ), several works show that many kernel matrices behave like polynomial kernels of
degree k (with rigorous deterministic equivalents and sharp asymptotics) (Xiao et al., 2022; Lu and
Yau, 2025; Cheng and Montanari, 2024; Misiakiewicz and Saeed, 2024). In the quadratic regime
(k = 2), nonlinear kernels can reduce in operator norm to quadratic polynomial kernels (Ghorbani
et al., 2019b; Pandit et al., 2024), enabling classification of quadratically separable data such as XOR
(Refinetti et al., 2021). Wen et al. (2025) recently proved a conditional Gaussian equivalence for
random feature model at quadratic regime to show the asymptotic generalization error in this case.
Gaussian mixtures and XOR problem. Gaussian mixture classification, specifically the XOR
mixture has become an important testbed for statistics and ML to evaluate various algorithms.
Refinetti et al. (2021) documented a sharp contrast between trained two-layer networks and kernel
methods on such mixtures, motivating a spectral analysis of when (and why) kernels can succeed.
Related RMT analyses for mixture classification with kernels appear in (Liao and Couillet, 2019;
Couillet, 2019). Glasgow (2023) showed how training two layer NNs with SGD can learn this XOR
problem even with a sample complexity Õ(d). Recently, Taheri et al. (2025) analyzed continual
learning by studying one-hidden-layer quadratic NNs trained with gradient descent on an XOR
dataset. Demir and Dogan (2025) analyzed two-layer networks after one gradient step on W with
Gaussian-mixture data using higher-order polynomial equivalence. This motivates our spiked feature
case in Section 4.3, while our result focuses on label-aligned outliers for linear classification on XOR,
unlike trained feature regression tasks in Demir and Dogan (2025).

4. Main Results
We now present our main results on the outlier eigenvalues and eigenvectors of K across the
regimes summarized in Table 1. In the first three regimes, we consider proportional limit, where
d, n, N → ∞ proportionally: Section 4.1 studies finite SNR = Θ(1) regime; Section 4.2 analyzes
large SNR = Θ(n1/4 ) case; and Section 4.3 replaces the random weight W with a pretrained weight.
Then, Section 4.4 considers the quadratic sample-size regime n ≍ d2 , with finite SNR and random
weights. In each case, we predict the emergence of spikes of K and whether their eigenvectors
enable linear classification of X.

4.1. Proportional Limit with Finite SNR Case

is finite. We show that the outlier eigenvectors cannot be used to linearly classify the dataset, even
partially.

4.2. Large-SNR Proportional Limit Case
Theorem 3 shows that spectral methods based on outlier eigenvectors fail to linearly classify XOR
in the finite-SNR proportional regime. Linear informative spikes may still emerge, but a purely
linear approximation of σ cannot capture the quadratic feature needed for XOR. To make XOR
linearly learnable, we now increase the SNR so that the quadratic Hermite component of σ becomes
non-vanishing. Then two outliers created by the quadratic component become label-informative,
enabling linear classification. Numerical simulations of all these cases are in Appendix B.

5. Conclusion
We introduce a quadratic equivalent framework and illustrate its use by characterizing when nonlinear
structure becomes spectrally visible in the CK matrix. For the nonlinear XOR problem, we show
that in the proportional limit with finite SNR, the CK can exhibit outliers, but their eigenvectors
are asymptotically unaligned with labels. In contrast, increasing SNR, moving to the quadratic
sample-size regime, or adding pretrained structure to the weights can make the quadratic feature
non-negligible and produce informative outliers that enable linear spectral classification. Our results
highlight the complex and subtle relationship between common ML training “knobs” and the
emergence of spikes in the spectrum of ML models. Extending QE to more general scalings, deeper
networks, and other forms of structured data is an interesting direction.

Appendix B. Numerical Simulations: Varying Knobs
We now present numerical simulations that validate and complement the theoretical predictions in
Section 4.

Baseline case: proportional limit with finite SNR. Figure 1 shows the random CK spectra for
the XOR model in the finite-SNR regime and proportional limit (Assumption 2), together with the
theoretical spike predictions from Theorem 3. For the activation function used in this simulation,
uninformative spikes described in Theorem 3(ii) do not appear. Consistent with Theorem 3(iii)–(iv),
the two leading eigenvalues are outliers, and their eigenvectors exhibit nontrivial alignment with
v1 and v2 , defined in (3.6), while remaining asymptotically orthogonal to the XOR label vector y.
Consequently, although one could potentially apply downstream nonlinear transformations to these
leading eigenvectors to classify the data, direct linear classification of the XOR problem from the CK
eigenvectors fails in this regime.
    This setting serves as our baseline. The theoretical results in Section 4 identify four primary
control parameters, or “knobs,” that govern the emergence of CK outliers and the alignment of
their eigenvectors with the XOR labels y: (1) the SNR r2 ; (2) the choice of nonlinearity σ, through
the constants (bσ , cσ ) defined in (3.2) and (3.3); (3) the weight structure, comparing random and
pretrained weights; and (4) the asymptotic scaling regime relating (n, d, N ). Below, we vary these
knobs one at a time to isolate their effects on the CK spectrum relative to this baseline.


B.1. Knob I: SNR of the XOR Dataset

if cσ ̸= 0, making linear classification of XOR possible through (4.13) in Theorem 7(iv). When
moving from Figure 1 to Figure 2, we only increase the SNR from 36 to 1225. This change produces
two additional outliers, one of whose eigenvectors asymptotically aligns with the XOR labels y.
